page.title: Migration
page.description: Move running actors to a chart's new version, each at rest, keeping its session, states and queue while the host goes on working.

hero.headline: Move running actors to a new version.
hero.lede: A migration moves each actor to its chart's new version when it is at rest, keeping its session, states, queue and delayed sends. Two million actors, most of them hibernated, moved while events kept coming.

section.heading: Deploy without stopping long-lived actors.
section.p: An order that waits a week for its delivery is still running when the chart's next version ships. Stopping it would lose its state.
A migration moves it instead, while the host goes on working. It is part of operating a host.

section.heading: Each image adds a segment.
section.p: Each image makes a new segment of the host: those new Host was given, and each host.addImage(image) after.
An image that holds a chart whose name the host has gives that chart a new version. host.spawn(name) spawns the newest, which host.chart(name) returns.
So actors spawned from then on run the new version, and the running ones stay on theirs.
Adding the image is a deploy on its own: an actor that may finish on its version needs no migration.
An actor found by name is replaced when its owner spawns the new version under the name (updating through names). Migrate the actors that must not wait for their end.

section.heading: The upgrade event carries the old variables.
section.p: host.migrate() moves the running actors to the newest version of their chart, during the next turns.
A moved actor keeps its session, its active states, its queue and its delayed sends with their data. Its states are matched by id (below).
Its variables do not carry over by themselves, since the new version may name them differently. The actor first gets error.platform.upgrade, whose data holds the old version's variables.
Version 2 of this counter renames n to count and takes the old value from the upgrade event:

example.code: v1 counts 1 v1 counts 2 started migration 1 session 1 moved to segment 1 migration 1: 1 moved, 0 failed upgraded, the old variables were {"n":2} v2 counts 12

section.p: Once no actor runs on an old segment, the host retires it and frees its memory. host.hostStats counts the retired segments ().

section.heading: A migration runs no <onentry>.
section.p: A migration is not a transition. It enters the new version's states without their <onentry>, and leaves the old without their <onexit>.
The states are matched by id, and the configuration is completed to a legal one:

item.text: a state that is compound in the new version, and had no children in the old, is entered at its initial child, or its first;
a state the new version does not have at all is replaced by its parent's initial state, the chart's initial at the top;
a <parallel> gets all its regions, and an <invoke> of a state the migration enters is started.

section.p: So what an <onentry> would have done, such as arming a timer or telling your program, is the upgrade transition's job. In() tells it where the actor landed.
Version 2 of this subscription gives pastDue a grace period and drops paused:

example.code: 1 upgraded into grace: arming its timer 2 upgraded into active 1n {"pastDue":"grace"} 2n "active" next deadline 7000

section.p: grace onentry is never logged. Without the upgrade transition's <send>, actor 1 would wait in grace forever.

section.heading: One call starts it, two handlers report.

item.text: starts a migration and returns its id, a number. With no options it moves the actors of every chart; chart names one chart, session one actor. wake: true asks for the hibernated actors. timeout is in milliseconds of the host's clock, rounded up to its next tick; 0 or none means none. A chart the host does not have throws TA_ERROR_INVALID, and a session that ended TA_ERROR_STALE: a migration that could move nothing is refused rather than reported done.

in the host's options, gets the end of each migration: { migration, migrated, failed, pending }. failed lists the actors it could not move, each { session, reason } with reason core's status; pending lists the sessions (bigints) its timeout left behind. It is a handler of the host, so a migration started by a host that was later restored reports to the restored host's handler.
gets each actor moved, a view of session, segment, chart (its name) and migration, valid while the handler runs.

section.heading: Give a migration a timeout.
section.p: A migration ends when every actor it looks at has moved, or at its timeout.
An actor running an invocation, an invoked chart or a service, moves once the invocation ends. With a timeout the migration waits for that until the timeout.
Without a timeout it fails such an actor at once with 'TA_ERROR_STATE', since an invocation may never end.
A hibernated actor moves once it is woken. With wake: true the migration asks the host for it, and the host loads it from its store.
The migration asks again if it finds the actor hibernated after a wake.
Without wake, a hibernated actor that nothing wakes holds the migration until its timeout. Without a timeout it holds it forever, and migrationDone is never called.
A migration still running when the host is closed never reaches migrationDone.

section.heading: An actor that cannot be written out stays.
section.p: Such an actor stays on its version, in the result's failed with reason 'TA_ERROR_UNSUPPORTED'. host.hibernate of the actor names the variable.
On the native datamodel, its variables hold a value outside the value table: a function, a Map, a Date.
Hibernation refuses the same actors.
On the native datamodel the upgrade event's data holds exactly the old version's variables. The old names the new version does not declare are gone.
The actor gets the new version's helpers. The new version's vars are declared and undefined, since a migration runs no script.

section.heading: A resident bound paces a large migration.
section.p: A migration with wake: true asks for every hibernated actor early. Woken all at once, they would all be in memory at once.

A host with a resident bound loads a migration's requests only while it holds fewer actors than the bound. It hibernates actors again after each turn, so the migration moves the population a few at a time.
An event's request still loads its actor at once.
A hundred counters with resident: 10 migrate with at most 10 in memory between turns:

example.code: 90 hibernated 100 moved, 0 failed, at most 10 in memory between turns

section.heading: Two million actors migrated with 1000 resident.
section.p: tools/migration.mjs (mise run migration) runs this pattern at scale, with the actors past the bound in SQLite.
200,000 events came before the migration and 200,000 more during it. Every actor moved to version 2 with wake: true, in 3,688,635 loads from the store per run.
Every actor migrated, none failed and none was left. All 25,000 sampled actors had their count and version 2, and version 1's segment was retired.
After every eviction at most 1000 actors were resident.

table.caption: Two million actors of version 1 of a counter, at most 1000 resident, the rest in SQLite, all moved to version 2. One run of tools/migration.mjs, alone on the machine, 2026-11-20: Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, 4 CPUs, 16 GiB, Linux; Node.js 22.23.5, Bun 1.4.1.
